title: Users Query
statement:
An HR API serves GET /users?min=&max=&offset=&limit=&sort=. Query-string values always arrive as strings, so the endpoint must validate them before it can filter, sort and page.

Write def solution(users, params). users is a list of [name, salary] (unique names, salary a number). params is a dict of strings; any key may be missing.

  • min (default "0") and max (default "4000"): decimal numbers, meaning an optional -, digits, and optionally . plus digits. max is also illegal when it is less than min.
  • offset (default "0") and limit (default: no limit): whole numbers ≥ 0, digits only.
  • sort: NAME or SALARY, any case. Missing means keep the given order.
  • A param that is present but empty is illegal.

If any param is illegal, return {"error": name} for the first illegal one in the order min, max, offset, limit, sort.

Otherwise keep users with min ≤ salary ≤ max, sort them (by name, or by salary with ties broken by name), then skip offset rows and keep at most limit. Return {"results": [[name, salary], ...]}.

examples.why: Defaults are min 0, max 4000, no sort. Bob earns 4500, so he is filtered out; the rest keep their order.
Eve is under 1000 and Bob over 4000. Sorted by salary: Alex and Dina tie on 1500, so name decides. limit 2 keeps the first two.
Both are numbers, but max is below min, so max is the illegal param.

constraints: params keys are a subset of min, max, offset, limit, sort; values are strings of length ≤ 20

think.q: What are the four stages, and in what order?
think.a: Validate, filter, sort, page. Paging must come last: limit 2 means the first two rows of the sorted, filtered list, not two random users.
Filter keeps all three. Sort by (salary, name): B 3, A 5, C 5. Skip one: [['A', 5], ['C', 5]].
It crashes on a missing key and on "abc", and int("-1") succeeds even though a negative limit is illegal. float() also accepts "1e3" and "nan". Write small explicit validators.
"sort by", "ties", "offset", "limit" → sorting with a tuple key, then slicing. key=lambda r: (r[1], r[0]) sorts by salary and breaks ties by name in one pass.

1. Read each param with its default; validate in order min, max, offset, limit, sort; return the first error.
  2. Filter lo <= salary <= hi.
  3. Sort if asked.
  4. Slice rows[offset : offset + limit], or rows[offset:] with no limit.

Empty DB. Offset past the end (empty list, not an error). limit=0. min == max. Two illegal params (name the first). sort=salary in lower case. ?sort= with an empty value. A salary equal to max (inclusive).

hints: Use params.get('min', '0') for defaults, and keep params.get('limit') as None to mean "no limit".
Validate in the order the spec gives and return on the first failure. For offset and limit, "digits only" rejects -1, 1.5 and the empty string in one check.
Sort by salary with rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r[1], r[0])), then slice with rows[start:end] where end is None when there is no limit.
explain:
The function is a pipeline: validate → filter → sort → page. Most bugs come from doing these in the wrong order or from trusting int()/float() as validators.

  • Example 2: min is "1000", max defaults to "4000", offset to "0", limit is "2", sort upper-cases to SALARY. All legal.
  • Filter keeps Carol 3200, Alex 1500, Dina 1500.
  • Sort by (salary, name): Alex 1500, Dina 1500, Carol 3200.
  • Slice [0:2]: Alex and Dina.

In the take-home this sits behind Express. In an interview, say that the same pipeline maps to SQL: WHERE salary BETWEEN $1 AND $2 ORDER BY salary, name OFFSET $3 LIMIT $4, and that the tie-breaker is what makes pages stable.
complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort (O(n) without sort), O(n) extra space for the filtered rows

tests.why: defaults are min 0, max 4000, no sort: Bob (4500) is filtered out, order is kept

tests.label: example 2 (sort, then limit)
tests.why: Alex and Dina tie on 1500, so the tie breaks by name; limit keeps the first 2

tests.label: example 3 (min above max)
tests.why: max is illegal when it is below min

tests.label: empty DB
tests.why: no users gives an empty list, not an error

tests.label: max is inclusive
tests.why: a salary equal to the default max of 4000 is included

tests.label: sort by name, page 2
tests.why: sort is case-insensitive; offset 1 skips Alex

tests.label: offset past the end
tests.why: slicing past the end gives an empty list, not an error

tests.label: limit zero
tests.why: a limit of 0 is legal and returns nothing

tests.label: min equals max
tests.why: both ends are inclusive, decimals are fine

tests.label: negative offset
tests.why: offset must be a whole number >= 0

tests.label: two illegal params
tests.why: min is checked before sort, so the error names min

tests.label: fractional limit
tests.why: limit must be a whole number; it is checked before sort

tests.label: empty sort value
tests.why: a param that is present but empty (?sort=) is illegal

tests.label: salary ties, mid page
tests.why: three people on 2000 sort Ann, Kim, Lee; offset 1 drops Raj

perf.label: performance: 20,000 users, sort by salary, one page

govtech.evidence: A 2025 copy of the take-home spec (github.com/bryanlohxz/swe-take-home-assignment, which says it is adapted from GovTech ACE hiring) and a candidate's March 2025 solution (github.com/tjingsheng/swe-take-home-assignment) define GET /users with min (default 0.0), max (default 4000.0), offset, limit and sort=NAME|SALARY; the spec leaves min > max, salary ties and the error body open (that candidate returned an empty list for min > max), so those rules are this exercise's choice.
extensions: OFFSET 100000 makes the DB read and throw away 100,000 rows, and rows shift if someone inserts while you page. Switch to keyset pagination: WHERE (salary, name) > ($last_salary, $last_name) ORDER BY salary, name LIMIT 20.
Which index makes WHERE salary BETWEEN ... ORDER BY salary, name fast? A composite index on (salary, name) serves the filter, the sort and the tie-breaker without a separate sort step.
Return a total count with each page so the UI can show "page 3 of 40". Count after filtering but before paging, and discuss what an exact COUNT(*) costs on millions of rows.
Return 400 with a message per bad param instead of just the first one, e.g. {"errors": {"limit": "must be a whole number"}}. Collect every error rather than returning early.
